title: When a Website Is the Job, and When It Isn't
description: A marketing site and custom software solve different problems. Here's how to tell which one your Treasure Valley business actually needs.
author: Erik Short
markdown:
## Quick answers

- **Is a website the same thing as custom software?** No. A website gets you found and makes a good first impression; custom software is the system your business runs on day to day.
- **When does a business need a website instead of custom software?** When the problem is that people can't find you, don't trust you yet, or need a place to see what you sell — not when the problem is internal work breaking down.
- **Can one business need both?** Yes, and often does — a site for the public, a separate system for the operation behind it.
- **What does a website from Idaho Software Development include?** Design and build of a marketing site — services pages, a portfolio, or an online store — handed over ready to use.
- **Does a website fix a spreadsheet or scheduling mess?** No. That's a custom software problem, not a website problem, even though both get lumped together as "we need something online."

## Two different jobs that look like one

People call asking for "a website" and what they actually need is a system. Or they ask about "software" when what's really missing is a page that tells people who they are and how to reach them. The words get used interchangeably, but the jobs are not the same, and building the wrong one wastes money either way.

Here's the simple version: a website is for people outside your business who don't know you yet. Custom software is for the work inside your business that keeps it running. One is about being found and taken seriously. The other is about the actual operation — the jobs, the schedules, the customers, the data you're currently keeping track of in a spreadsheet, a notebook, or a string of texts.

## What a website is for

A website's job is narrow, and that's a feature, not a limitation. It needs to:

- Show up when someone searches for what you do
- Explain what you offer clearly enough that a stranger trusts you
- Give people a way to contact you, book you, or buy from you
- Look like a real, established business — because for a lot of customers, your site is the first and only impression they get before they decide whether to call

That's it. A services site, a portfolio, an online store — these are all variations on the same job: put your best foot forward in public. [Ridgeline Integrated Systems](/) and [High Desert Dairy Lab](/) are examples of businesses that needed exactly that — a site that represents them well and gets handed over ready to use.

A website does not need to track your job queue. It doesn't need to know which customer is overdue on an invoice or which crew is scheduled where tomorrow. If you're asking your website to do that, you're asking the wrong tool to do a job it was never built for.

## What custom software is for

Custom software is for the parts of the business that only your business does, in exactly the way your business does them. It's the internal tool that replaces the spreadsheet everyone's afraid to touch. It's the customer portal that stops the back-and-forth emails. It's the system that tracks jobs, people, inventory, or scheduling the way your operation actually works — not the way some off-the-shelf app assumes it should work.

The tell that you've outgrown general tools and need something built for you specifically is usually the same: a spreadsheet that's grown so many tabs and side-conversations that no one fully trusts it anymore. If that sounds familiar, it's worth reading through [when a Treasure Valley business has outgrown its spreadsheets](/blog/when-a-treasure-valley-business-has-outgrown-its-spreadsheets) — it covers the signs in more detail.

Custom software at this shop starts as a written scope and ends as a system in use, with the shop staying involved after launch. It's not a marketing exercise. It's infrastructure. Some systems the shop has running — Job Workflow Pro, UmpCrew, Camp HQ, DugoutIQ — are built around a specific operation's actual workflow, not a generic template with your logo on it. If you're getting ready to start one, [what to send when you start a custom software project](/blog/what-to-send-when-you-start-a-custom-software-project) walks through what makes that first conversation productive.

## How to tell which one you need

Ask what's actually broken.

- If the problem is "people don't know we exist" or "we look unprofessional online" or "we have no way for someone to buy from us" — that's a website problem.
- If the problem is "we're losing track of jobs," "our team is re-entering the same data three times," or "customers keep calling because they can't see their own status" — that's a custom software problem.
- If the problem is both — your public presence is thin *and* your internal operation runs on duct tape — you may need both, but they're still two separate pieces of work, not one project pretending to be the other.

A lot of businesses reasonably want to solve everything at once. That's understandable, but it usually leads to an expensive site that tries to also be a database, or software that gets treated like a brochure and never actually used the way it was built to be used. Keeping the two separate, even when you need both, keeps each one doing its actual job.

## What this shop will and won't do

Websites here are the smaller, separate offer: a marketing site designed and built, then handed over ready to use. Services pages, portfolios, online stores — [Legacy Feed and Fuel](/) is an example of that kind of site. What it won't do is pretend a website can replace a system your team needs to run the business on. If what you actually need is custom software, that's a different conversation, with a different starting point — a written scope, not a page layout.

Likewise, if all you need is to be found and taken seriously online, you don't need a six-figure internal system. You need a well-built site that does its one job well. Matching the tool to the actual problem is most of what good advice looks like here.

## Frequently asked questions

### When does a business need a website instead of custom software?
When the problem is external — being found, looking credible, giving people a way to reach or buy from you. If the problem is internal, like scheduling, tracking jobs, or managing customer data, that's a custom software problem even if it also involves a screen.

### What does Idaho Software Development include when it builds a website?
Design and build of a marketing site — services pages, a portfolio, or an online store — handed over ready to use. It's a separate, smaller offer from custom software, which involves a written scope and ongoing involvement after launch.

### Can a website eventually grow into needing custom software too?
Yes, this happens often. A business starts with a site to be found, grows, and then the internal operation outgrows spreadsheets and email. At that point it's a second, separate project, not a rebuild of the website.

### Does a bigger website with more pages solve operational problems?
No. Adding pages, a blog, or a fancier design to a marketing site doesn't fix a tracking or scheduling problem. Those need a system built around how the work actually happens, which is what custom software is for.

### Is it cheaper to just ask for "a website" and have it do everything?
It rarely works out cheaper. A site stretched to do a system's job tends to need rebuilding later anyway, once the limits show up. Separating the two from the start usually saves money, not costs more.

If you're not sure which one you need, that's a fine place to start — [reach out](/#start) and describe the problem, not the solution, and we'll help you figure out which one it actually is.
